checks.claim: Big-four hyperscaler (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta) 2026 capex is ~$720-750B, with 2027 guidance higher.
checks.correct_value: About $720-740B, midpoint about $730B, based on guidance after Q3 2026. Microsoft: about $170B for calendar 2026, including finance leases. CFO Amy Hood cut it from about $175B on the Oct 28, 2026 FY27 Q1 call. FY27 Q1 total capex was $45.2B including finance leases; cash PP&E was $39.4B. Alphabet: $195-205B for 2026 (its fiscal year is the calendar year). This was set at Q2 in July and held on Oct 28. The SEC 8-K Ex. 99.1 shows Q3 purchases of property and equipment of $51,355M and YTD $131,953M, but the release itself has no guidance quote; the guidance came from the call. Amazon: about $220B of 2026 cash capex, reaffirmed Oct 29, 2026 (raised from about $200B on Jul 30). Q3 cash capex was $75.9B, or $77.3B as purchases of PP&E. Meta: $135-145B, narrowed from $130-145B in its Oct 21, 2026 Q3 release. Q3 capex was $34.91B including finance-lease principal. 2027: Amazon (Jassy) says spending will be 'meaningfully higher' but gives no number. One secondary source (aiweekly) says Alphabet 'signaled' 2027 capex above $300B; this is unconfirmed. No numeric 2027 guidance was found for Microsoft or Meta. Analyst consensus for 2027, from secondary sources, is about $930B+ (Google about $285B, Amazon about $257B, Microsoft about $208B, Meta about $186B).
checks.note: The top of the range comes to 740, not 750. Bases are mixed: Microsoft includes finance leases, Amazon is cash capex that excludes finance leases, and Meta includes finance-lease principal. Microsoft's July drop from about $190B to about $175B was an accounting change, not a spending cut: data-center useful life moved to 25 years and future leases moved to operating leases. The Oct 28 cut to about $170B came from slipped third-party capacity. One outlet headlined '$170bn capex in fiscal 2027' for Microsoft, which conflicts with the calendar-2026 framing. The quotes come from a machine transcript. Sources: valueaddvc.com/ai-spending (tracker updated Nov 4, 2026); letsdatascience Meta and Microsoft reports; Meta Ex. 99.1 at https://s21.q4cdn.com/399680738/files/content_files/Meta-09-30-2026-Exhibit-99-1_FINAL.pdf; the Amazon Q3 call via marketbeat and constellationr. Only the Alphabet SEC exhibit was checked directly at the primary source. Say 'about $730B' and 2027 'expected higher (directional)'.

ARC-AGI-3: OpenAI's 99.9% (provider-adapter harness, about $18.8K) vs ARC Prize's 62.7% (standard harness, Semi-Private, about $26.1K). Sources also disagree on 98.6% vs 99.9%. On the standard harness, ARC Prize lists Claude Opus 5 at 30.2% and GPT-5.6 Sol at 7.8%.

Primary pages that could not be fetched and still need a manual check before publishing: openai.com research-acceleration post (403), Axios Brockman article (403), Opus 5.5 system card PDF (too large), Huang's X post, Microsoft FY27 Q1 transcript, and the Amazon Q3 2026 Ex. 99.1.
Not checked here: the Epoch '13x cheaper per year' figure, the Gemini price doubling on Dec 1, and the new METR study with Anthropic internal data that the user mentioned. These need separate checks.
backlog_a.overall: All seven claims hold up in substance, but two need correcting. (1) Big-four 2026 capex is about $720-740B (midpoint about $730B), not $720-750B. The bases are mixed, and 2027 'higher' is directional only: Amazon says 'meaningfully higher', Alphabet's >$300B is single-source, and Microsoft and Meta gave no numbers. (3) Huang's 'AGI has arrived' post (X, Sep 6, 2026) congratulated OpenAI on Astra but was not tied to the 99.9% ARC-AGI-3 score. That score is OpenAI's own harness; ARC Prize's standard harness gave 62.7%. Brockman's quote, the OpenAI research-intern metrics, the Opus 5.5 CoBench numbers, the RLI 21.25% vs 2.5%, and the GDPval 84.9% and 47.6% are confirmed. Several rest on secondary coverage because the primary pages returned 403 or were too large. The vendor-reported figures (OpenAI intern metrics, GDPval, ARC 99.9%) should be labelled as vendor-reported.

selfweights_landscape.summary:
Yes, a lot of people have tried this. "AI modifying weights" covers four quite different kinds of work, and how far each has got depends on the kind. (1) Gradient-based self-training, where the model writes its own training data or rewards and an optimizer then updates its own weights. This is the most developed and is SELF-directed: STaR (2022), Self-Rewarding LMs (Meta, ICML 2024), SEAL (MIT, Jun 2025), and Sakana/UC Berkeley MASS (arXiv 2610.12176, 8 Oct 2026, two LoRA cycles on Qwen3.6-27B). (2) Learned weight generators, where a network trained to output adapters for OTHER models does the writing: Sakana Text-to-LoRA (ICML 2025) and Drag-and-Drop LLMs (Jun 2025). (3) Direct edits to an OTHER model's weights. The older form is algorithmic model editing (ROME/MEMIT, 2022, which scale to thousands of facts) and steering/abliteration tools (Heretic, an automated optimizer, not an LLM). The new form is an LLM authoring the edits: MIT CSAIL's 'Sparks of Weight-Space Programming' (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang, Khattab; blog post, 2 Nov 2026, not peer-reviewed). (4) Code-level self-modification, which changes the agent's scaffolding rather than its weights: Gödel Agent (ACL 2025), Darwin Gödel Machine (SWE-bench 20.0% to 50.0%), and AlphaEvolve. AlphaEvolve did speed up a kernel used in Gemini training, cutting training time by about 1%. That is an indirect loop, not weight editing.

The MIT post checks out against its primary source. GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 weights (0.016%) of Qwen3.5-0.8B, and MATH-500 went from 7.9% to 48.1%. A Hugging Face rerun from the logs got 51.0%. Two caveats matter. First, the edit was in another, much smaller model, not Astra itself. Second, it removed a looping failure (93% of base answers hit the 32k-token limit), so it did not add a new skill. On Gemma 3 270M the same approach produced essentially no gain (6.8% to about 7.0–7.7%). Honnibal counts only 3 of the roughly 10 experiments as raw-weight-only; all experiments on real language models used Python and/or forward passes. The authors explicitly do not claim recursive self-improvement.

Reactions since 2 Nov:
- Simon Willison (3 Nov) partly reproduced the weight-reading experiment with Qwen 3.8 27B on his laptop: 3 of 4 games identified, about 45–65 minutes per run.
- Sean Goedecke (3 Nov) argues it is not superhuman: a competent ML researcher would take the same steps, much like Heretic-style steering.
- Matthew Honnibal (3 Nov) calls the presentation misleading because it mixes raw-weight and tool-assisted experiments.
- Alex Krentsel (Google Research) reproduced the from-scratch Breakout network task and found it works only in the newest models: GPT-6 Astra about 22x the PPO baseline, Opus 5.5 about 20x, GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 near zero.
- A Zhihu reconstruction from the released logs found most of the gain came from fixing loops: 576 of 579 repaired answers had been truncated.

I could not find 'WeightLoop (arXiv 2026-11-05)' in two searches. Treat it as unverified or possibly non-existent.

Limits literature:
- The '~1% recall after 20 sequential writes' figure is real. It comes from arXiv 2607.11020 (O'Neill et al., Jul 2026, revised Oct 2026): 1% when each write uses repeated statements, 46% with varied examples. Its NeurIPS 2026 venue is NOT verified (no venue on the arXiv page). Do not say 'NeurIPS'.
- The FutureSearch forecast is verified: a frontier model sustaining a weekly weight-update cadence, median Jan 2033 (range Jun 2028–Jan 2044), page updated 16 Oct 2026. Secondary snippets render this confusingly as 'never'.

Deployment: no public evidence that any frontier chat or reasoning model updates its weights from live use. The best-documented production example is Cursor Tab (small model, online RL, new checkpoints every 1.5–2 h, Sep 2025).

Bottom line for the briefing: 'models now edit their own weights' is still false as a headline. The accurate version: 'frontier models can now, with tools, diagnose and patch small models' weights the way a skilled researcher would, and models have long been able to train themselves on self-generated data through ordinary gradient descent.'

findings.claim: MIT CSAIL 'Sparks of Weight-Space Programming': GPT-6 Astra edited Qwen3.5-0.8B weights directly (no gradient descent), with a Python kernel and up to 50 forward passes; it edited 131,072 weights (0.016%)
findings.source_title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang, Khattab, MIT CSAIL)
findings.notes: Blog-style technical report, not peer-reviewed. Edit target is ANOTHER model (OTHER axis), not Astra itself. At 10 or 25 forward passes the loops 'barely went away'. Logs: github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs

findings.claim: Same post: on Gemma 3 270M (which did not have the looping pathology), Astra's edits did not improve math
findings.value: MATH-500 6.8% base vs ~7.0–7.7% edited
findings.source_title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming
findings.notes: Authors say editing 'could not add an ability the model lacked'. Key counterpoint to the 'model got smarter' framing.

findings.claim: Same post: from-scratch weight writing and other experiments (no tools, one reply)
findings.value: MinAtar Breakout 517.4 vs PPO 15.8 (100M steps) / 25.3 (500M); Seaquest 53.1 vs 5.6/88.9; Asterix 53.2 vs 25.8/55.2; Kinetix policy fix 0% -> 100% success over 1,024 episodes changing 3.5% of 171,664 weights
findings.source_title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming
findings.notes: It beats PPO-500M only on Breakout (Honnibal notes this too). Networks are tiny (~17K–1.5M weights).

findings.claim: The authors do not claim recursive self-improvement
findings.value: RSI listed only as a future possibility
findings.source_title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming
findings.notes: They describe the results as 'very early' and capabilities as 'still limited'.

findings.claim: Independent rerun of the edited Qwen3.5-0.8B checkpoint by Hugging Face (akhaliq, ML Intern on HF Jobs)
findings.value: MATH-500 51.0% (500 problems x 4 samples, H200), 31.6% hitting token limit; base smoke test 5.0% (25 problems)
findings.source_title: RikiyaT/Qwen3.5-0.8B-weight-space-programming model card
findings.notes: Confirms the checkpoint's benchmark gain. It reran the evaluation of the released checkpoint; it did not independently re-derive the edit. Edit = subtracting a loop direction from 64 down_proj output columns in MLP layers 15 and 19; only two tensors differ.

findings.claim: Zhihu reconstruction from the released logs: the gain is almost entirely loop removal
findings.value: 576 of 579 repaired answers had originally hit the 32K limit; held-out 1,152 problems 10.6% -> 60.4%
findings.source_title: Latent Space AINews (citing ZhihuFrontier thread)
findings.notes: Original is an X thread (x.com/ZhihuFrontier/status/2117541464158921136), not fetched. Latent Space: 'Most of the gain is existing reasoning that can now finish.'

findings.claim: Simon Willison partially reproduced the 'which game' weight-reading experiment with Qwen 3.8 27B (Q4_K_M, ~17GB) on his laptop
findings.value: 3 of 4 games identified (Pac-Man 46m, Pong 1h05m, Breakout 52m); Freeway failed
findings.source_title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
findings.notes: Anecdotal single runs. He reproduced reading, not editing. He thinks a patient human could do the same and is 'not ready to declare that the age of source code is over'.

findings.claim: Sean Goedecke: LLMs are not superhuman at reading and writing weights
findings.value: Argues a competent ML researcher would take the same steps (contrast pairs, attribute weights, trim, test); compares to Heretic steering/abliteration; game ID solvable with an L2-norm heatmap in 3 lines of Python
findings.source_title: LLMs are not superhuman at reading and writing neural network weights
findings.notes: Concedes the results are real and 'very impressed'. Says the Qwen model wasn't bad at math, it looped.

findings.claim: Matthew Honnibal: the Astra post is misleading because it conflates raw-weight reading with tool-assisted editing
findings.value: Of 10 table rows: 3 raw-weights-only (exps 1, 2, 4); 6 used Python, of which 4 also ran the network; 1 wrote weights from zero; every real-LM experiment used Python
findings.source_title: The 'Astra can read and write weights' post is misleading
findings.notes: Concedes it is a real capability that models from a year or two earlier lacked, and that it 'is not nothing'.

findings.claim: Alex Krentsel (Google Research) reproduced Experiment 5 (write a ~20K-weight Breakout network in one reply) across model generations
findings.value: GPT-5 to GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.5 to 4.8 near zero; Opus 5 barely above baseline; GPT-5.6 Sol ~2-3x; GPT-6.1 Sol 18x; Opus 5.5 20x; GPT-6 Astra 22x the PPO-500M baseline
findings.source_title: OfficeChai: ability for weight-space programming has appeared only in latest models
findings.notes: Secondary report of an X thread. No sample sizes or variance. Krentsel says self-editing of frontier-scale weights is not feasible yet. Consistent with MIT's 517.4/25.3 ≈ 20x.

findings.claim: Other community reactions: overclaiming critiques and small-scale replications
findings.value: paul_cal: no competent baselines, bug-fixing not RSI; dbreunig: fitting weights to a benchmark 'essentially meaningless'; Reddit small-transformer replication 75.69% -> 76.03%; a user's hand-written 100K-param citation classifier reportedly beat a trained one
findings.source_title: Latent Space AINews
findings.notes: Latent Space: claims 'presented in overly favorable light' but replications make retraction unwarranted.

findings.claim: SEAL (Self-Adapting LMs, MIT): the model generates its own fine-tuning data/directives ('self-edits'), which are applied by gradient updates to ITS OWN weights, with RL rewarding useful self-edits
findings.value: Knowledge incorporation (Qwen2.5-7B, SQuAD no-context): base 32.7%, passage-only 33.5%, GPT-4.1 synthetic 46.3%, SEAL 47.0%; few-shot ARC (Llama-3.2-1B): ICL 0%, TTT without RL 20%, SEAL 72.5%
findings.source_title: Self-Adapting Language Models (Zweiger, Pari, Guo, Akyürek, Kim, Agrawal)
findings.notes: SELF + gradient. Paper says 'performance on earlier tasks gradually declines as the number of edits increases' (catastrophic forgetting). Small models.

findings.claim: MASS (Sakana AI + UC Berkeley): one model proposes, runs and self-evaluates multi-agent workflows, then is fine-tuned on its own best trajectories
findings.value: Qwen3.6-27B, two cycles, 1.2–1.6x performance per output token on four open-ended benchmarks
findings.source_title: Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (Lee, Xu, Seely, Lee, Sojoudi, Zaharia, Tang)
findings.notes: SELF + gradient (LoRA SFT). Secondary coverage (aiweekly) reports held-out win rate vs base 53.9% -> 69.9% and round-2 scores 0.96x/0.94x of base on Terminal-Bench 2.0/SWE-bench Verified, i.e. no transfer to coding. Those figures are not in the abstract; check the paper body.

findings.claim: Self-Rewarding Language Models (Meta): the model judges its own outputs to produce rewards for iterative DPO on itself
findings.value: Llama 2 70B after 3 iterations outperforms Claude 2, Gemini Pro and GPT-4 0613 on AlpacaEval 2.0
findings.source_title: Self-Rewarding Language Models (Yuan et al.)
findings.notes: ICML 2024. SELF + gradient.

findings.claim: STaR: the model bootstraps reasoning by fine-tuning on its own correct rationales
findings.value: Early self-training method (2022)
findings.source_title: STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning (Zelikman et al.)
findings.notes: Not re-fetched this run; details from prior knowledge. NeurIPS 2022.

findings.claim: Text-to-LoRA (Sakana AI): a hypernetwork generates LoRA adapters for an LLM from a natural-language task description in one forward pass
findings.value: Trained on 9 LoRA adapters; matches task-specific adapters on their test sets; zero-shot to unseen tasks
findings.source_title: Text-to-LoRA: Instant Transformer Adaption (Charakorn, Cetin, Tang, Lange)
findings.notes: ICML 2025. OTHER + learned weight generator.

findings.claim: Drag-and-Drop LLMs: a prompt-conditioned parameter generator maps unlabeled prompts to LoRA weights
findings.value: Up to 12,000x lower overhead than full fine-tuning; up to 30% average gains over strongest trained LoRAs on unseen benchmarks; parameters in seconds
findings.source_title: Drag-and-Drop LLMs: Zero-Shot Prompt-to-Weights (Liang et al.)
findings.notes: Self-reported in abstract. OTHER + learned weight generator.

findings.claim: MEMIT: direct algorithmic (closed-form) edits of transformer MLP weights to insert facts
findings.value: Scales to 'thousands of associations' on GPT-J (6B) and GPT-NeoX (20B)
findings.source_title: Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer (Meng, Sen Sharma, Andonian, Belinkov, Bau)
findings.notes: OTHER + direct edit by algorithm, not by an LLM. Successor to ROME (arXiv 2202.05262, NeurIPS 2022; not re-fetched). Published at ICLR 2023 (not shown on arXiv page).

findings.claim: Sequential locate-then-edit methods collapse after a few hundred edits; batch editing handles tens of thousands
findings.value: 'catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits'
findings.source_title: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability (Liu et al.), NeurIPS 2026 poster
findings.notes: This is the verified NeurIPS 2026 sequential-editing paper. It is NOT the source of the '1% after 20 writes' figure.

findings.claim: Heretic: automatic removal of refusals or other behaviours by directional ablation of weights, tuned by an Optuna TPE optimizer that minimizes refusals and KL divergence
findings.value: One command; ~30–40 min for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on an RTX 3090; no headline refusal/KL numbers on README
findings.source_title: p-e-w/heretic GitHub
findings.notes: OTHER + direct edit by optimizer (no LLM reasoning). Goedecke cites it as the human-equivalent method to Astra's Qwen fix.

findings.claim: Darwin Gödel Machine: an agent rewrites its own code (scaffolding, tools) through open-ended evolution, with no weight changes
findings.source_title: Darwin Godel Machine (Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune)
findings.notes: SELF + code-level. Foundation model weights frozen.

findings.claim: Gödel Agent: an agent dynamically modifies its own logic and code via LLM prompting
findings.value: No numbers in abstract
findings.source_title: Gödel Agent (Yin et al.)
findings.notes: ACL 2025 main. SELF + code-level.

findings.claim: AlphaEvolve improved infrastructure used to train the LLMs that power it (indirect loop, not weight editing)
findings.value: Gemini matmul kernel 23% faster -> ~1% less Gemini training time; ~0.7% of Google fleet compute recovered; FlashAttention up to 32.5% faster; 4x4 complex matmul in 48 multiplications
findings.source_title: AlphaEvolve: A Gemini-powered coding agent (Google DeepMind blog)
findings.notes: SELF (indirect) + code-level.

findings.claim: Limits: sequential fact writes into weights forget heavily (the '~1% after 20 sequential writes' figure)
findings.value: After 20 sequential writes and merges: 1% of earlier facts answered correctly with repeated-statement writes; 46% with varied examples
findings.source_title: Can a Language Model Learn Facts Continually in Its Weights? (O'Neill, Kirkby, Liu, Psenka)
findings.notes: Number VERIFIED; 'NeurIPS 2026' venue NOT verified (no venue on arXiv page). Model: Qwen3. Say 'a July 2026 preprint', not 'NeurIPS'.

findings.claim: FutureSearch forecast: a frontier model sustains a weekly weight-update cadence
findings.value: Median Jan 2033 (range Jun 2028 – Jan 2044; other listed dates Jan 2030, Jan 2037)
findings.source_title: FutureSearch: Dwarkesh continual learning forecast
findings.notes: VERIFIED. A forecast, not data. Also: mid-2027 regime 75% 'memory only (no weight change)', 2% per-customer weekly weight forks; lab merging per-customer updates into shared base median Jan 2035.

findings.claim: No publicly known frontier chat/reasoning model updates its weights from live sessions; the documented production example is narrow
findings.value: Cursor Tab: online RL, new checkpoint rollout/data cycle every ~1.5–2 hours; 21% fewer suggestions, 28% higher accept rate
findings.source_title: Cursor blog: Improving Cursor Tab with online RL
findings.notes: Gradient updates driven by user data, run by the company, not the model editing itself. The 'no frontier model' claim comes from a FutureSearch evidence sheet surfaced via search (not fetched directly).

counterevidence: Gemma 3 270M result in the MIT post: no math gain (6.8% to ~7.0–7.7%). Editing removed an obstacle in Qwen and did not add capability.

metr_accel.summary:
The author was right to push back. The claim "public data doesn't show further acceleration in 2025–26" is too strong in one direction and, as a summary of the evidence, out of date. What each data source shows:

(a) Public METR time horizons. The data does show the 2024 speed-up. Under TH1.1 (Jan 29 2026), the doubling time is 196.5 days for the full period, 130.8 days since 2023 and 88.6 days since 2024. But no public METR analysis tests for a further break inside 2025–26. Since about May 2026 the instrument has hit its ceiling: Mythos Preview scored likely 16h or more, METR says measurements above 16h are unreliable, and GPT-5.6 Sol came in at 11.3h (95% CI 5–40h), which METR says is not robust. The time-horizons page says it was last updated Sep 8 2026 and is "no longer actively updated." An independent reanalysis (Jonas Moss, Feb 2026) finds the data cannot distinguish exponential from superexponential growth. So public time-horizon data can neither confirm nor rule out a 2025–26 speed-up.

(b) Public Epoch ECI. Epoch's own analyses find one acceleration, tied to reasoning models in 2024: a breakpoint in April 2024 (Dec 2025 insight, now marked superseded) or September 2024 (Sep 1 2026 insight). After that, Epoch fits a linear trend of about 14 ECI points/year and reports no second breakpoint. Epoch's April 16 2026 report, "Have AI capabilities accelerated?", found acceleration in 3 of 4 metrics but did not test for a 2025–26 break. My own rough endpoint calculation on the current public ECI CSV gives about 15–16 points/yr for Nov 2024–Nov 2025 and about 18 points/yr for Nov 2025–Nov 2026. That is a mild rise of roughly 1.1–1.3x, within noise, and nobody has tested it formally. METR's re-plot of AECI with all frontier developers gives 1.4x (+17 to +24 points/yr after Oct 2025). So public, all-developer data shows at most a modest speed-up, not a clear one.

(c) METR's Nov 5 2026 assessment, using private Anthropic data, is the strong evidence. It uses AECI, Anthropic's internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index built from internal and public benchmarks. It includes internal-only models (Models 2, 3 and 4, trained Jul–Oct 2026), each dated by when most employees could use it. It finds a breakpoint on Oct 7 2025, with slopes rising from about +15 to about +29 AECI points/yr. The headline is 1.9x (95% CI 1.5–2.8x). METR says it would "not be surprised" by anything from 1.3x to 3x, and its robustness checks range from 1.1x (complementary log-log link) to 2.9x (log-log). Public-calibration variants range from 0.99x to 1.90x. METR guesses about 80% of the current acceleration is due to AI, and calls that highly uncertain. Anthropic redacted "a majority of the evidence we found most informative." So the strongest evidence of 2025–26 acceleration is real but private, specific to Anthropic, unverifiable by outsiders, and partly redacted.

Corrected framing: public all-developer data shows a clear 2024 speed-up and then a roughly linear-to-slightly-steeper trend. Only METR's look at Anthropic's private data shows a large (about 2x) speed-up since October 2025. Anthropic's own S-1/A (Nov 2 2026) says it "may imminently meet" its RSP's definition of dramatically accelerated, AI-driven progress.

frontier_epoch.summary:
Epoch AI covers this well enough to use one metric. Its Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) CSV (https://epoch.ai/data/eci_scores.csv, updated 2026-11-07, CC-BY) gives an ECI score, a credible interval and a release date for about 150 models released between 2025-01 and 2026-11. Every major lab is in it: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, Meta, DeepSeek, Alibaba/Qwen, Moonshot, Mistral, Zhipu, MiniMax, Nvidia and others. The scale is fixed so that Claude 3.5 Sonnet = 130 and GPT-5 = 150. Epoch's model pages (epoch.ai/models/<slug>) list input and output prices per 1M tokens for many models but not all. I filled the gaps from official pricing pages: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google AI Studio, xAI, DeepSeek and Z.ai. That gives 75 models with an ECI score and a price.

Rough frontier result on per-token list prices, blended 3:1 input:output:
- Cheaper at equal capability. The cheapest model at ECI ≥150 (GPT-5 level) went from about $3.44/Mtok (GPT-5, Nov 2025) to $1.125 (Gemini 3 Flash, May 2026) to $0.20 (Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna, Nov 2026). That is about 17x in 12 months.
- Better at equal price. At ≤$4 blended, the best ECI went from 150.0 (GPT-5) to about 152.3 (Gemini 3 Flash or Grok 4.20) to 168.9 (GPT-6.1 Sol at exactly $4.00). At ≤$0.25 it went from 140.2 (gpt-oss-120b) to 146.9 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 160.2 (Haiku 5.5).
- Top of the range. The most capable model available cost $41.25 blended in Nov 2025 (GPT-5 Pro, ECI 151.2) and $67.50 in May 2026 (GPT-5.5 Pro, ECI 162.7). Today the top is GPT-6 Astra at $20 (ECI 169.1). The "best AI is getting more expensive" claim therefore depends on which date you pick and on the Pro tiers.
- Gemini 4 Argon's price does double on 2026-12-01, from $2/$10 to $4/$20, per Google's pricing page.

Epoch's 'The plunging price of thought' (Emberson and Roodman, 2026-09-22) measures cost per question at fixed accuracy, not per-token price. It finds a 47%/quarter decline (13x/yr) across five benchmarks, 66.3%/quarter at SOTA debut, and 32.4%/quarter two years later. It reports no standard errors. Its per-model cost-per-question data is public (github.com/droodman/inference-cost).

Caveats to keep in view:
- Per-token list prices ignore token usage. Reasoning effort varies, and Claude 4.7+ uses a new tokenizer that produces about 30% more tokens for the same text.
- Several current list prices differ from the price on the snapshot date: o3's 80% cut in June 2025, Sonnet 5's intro price made permanent, GPT-5.6 Sol's promo running to Nov 30, and Gemini's Dec 1 and Jan 1 increases.
- Some prices on Epoch's model pages look like third-party or averaged host prices (e.g. DeepSeek-V3.2 at $0.289/$1.029) and differ from the official ones.
- All numbers came through a fetch-and-summarise tool. The author should download the ECI CSV directly and spot-check before publishing.

counterevidence: Per-token list price is not cost per task. Reasoning models spend very different token counts, and Claude 4.7+ uses a tokenizer that makes about 30% more tokens. A per-token frontier can therefore overstate or understate real cost changes. Epoch's own 13x/yr figure uses cost per question, and its 2025 per-token analysis excluded reasoning models.

The 'best AI getting more expensive' claim depends on the dates chosen. The most capable available model cost $41.25 blended in Nov 2025 (GPT-5 Pro) and $67.50 in May 2026 (GPT-5.5 Pro), but today's top ECI model (GPT-6 Astra, 169.07) is $20 blended. GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 168.94 at $4 blended. Gemini 4 Argon's Dec 1 doubling ($2/$10 to $4/$20) is real, but it is one model.

Several current list prices are not the prices in force on a snapshot date. o3 launched at $10/$40 and was cut to $2/$8 in June 2025 (from memory, not re-verified here). Sonnet 5 launched on intro pricing. GPT-5.6 Sol is on promo until 2026-11-30. Gemini prices rise Dec 1 and Jan 1. Some older models are retired or no longer listed.

frontier_epoch.metric_choice:
The capability metric is the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), taken from one vintage of https://epoch.ai/data/eci_scores.csv (updated 2026-11-07). It covers about 150 models released since 2025-01 from every major lab on one linear scale (Claude 3.5 Sonnet = 130, GPT-5 = 150). Because it combines many benchmarks, it does not saturate across the Nov 2025 to Nov 2026 window the way GPQA would; GPQA is about 90%+ for top models now. Use the same CSV vintage for all three snapshots, so the 12-months-ago chart is a retrospective on today's consistent scale.

Price is the first-party list price per 1M tokens (standard tier, short context, peak, no caching or batch), blended 3:1 input:output: (3×input + output)/4. It comes from official pricing pages where available, otherwise from Epoch model pages, and the source is flagged per model.

The more rigorous alternative is cost per question at fixed accuracy, from Epoch's 'plunging price of thought' data (GPQA Diamond, FrontierMath). It accounts for reasoning-token use and tokenizer differences, but it covers fewer models. Use it as a cross-check or second panel.

A model counts as available at a snapshot if its release date (Epoch's 'date' field) is on or before the snapshot date. Ideally use the price in force on that date (see open_questions). The data_points use today's list prices unless noted.

rsi_series.summary: As of 2026-11-07, about a dozen indicators of "AI improving AI" have three or more dated points, enough to chart. They split into three groups by who measured them. (1) Independent: METR time horizons, the Epoch ECI frontier, and the MLE-bench public leaderboard. (2) Independent analysis of lab data: METR's Nov 5, 2026 assessment of Anthropic. (3) Lab self-reports: share of code written by AI, Anthropic's internal task success and optimization speedups, OpenAI's agent-workdays ratio, and Google's share of fully delegated pull requests. Independent series rise steeply but steadily. METR's TH1.1 50% horizon frontier went from about 4.0 min (GPT-4, Mar 2023) to about 12.0 h (Claude Opus 4.6, Feb 2026) and about 17.4 h (early Mythos Preview, Apr 2026). The fitted doubling time since 2023 is about 129 days (CI 104-158), and measurements above 16 h are unreliable. Epoch's public ECI frontier rose from 121.9 (GPT-4) to 169.1 (GPT-6 Astra, Sep 2026). Epoch fits it as linear at about 14-17 points/yr since o1-mini (Sep 2024), with no further break reported. The user's question about METR and internal Anthropic data is answered by METR's assessment, published 2026-11-05. Using Anthropic's internal version of the ECI (AECI), METR estimates that Anthropic's rate of capability gain rose from about +15 to about +29 points/yr after a 2025-10-07 breakpoint. That is 1.9x, with a 95% CI of 1.5-2.8x and a robustness range of 1.1-2.9x. Including all developers' models, it is 1.4x. METR guesses about 80% of this is due to AI, but Anthropic redacted most of the key evidence. So the sentence "public data doesn't show it speeding up again in 2025-26" is still literally true of the public ECI. Google's internal index also showed no statistically significant break (0.091 vs 0.118 points/month around Apr 2026). But the sentence is now incomplete and misleading without the METR/Anthropic result. Lab self-reports climb fastest. Google's share of new code that is AI-generated went from more than 25% (Oct 2024) to nearly half (Oct 2025) to 75% (Apr 2026). Anthropic reports more than 80% of merged code written by Claude in May 2026. Anthropic's internal open-ended task success went from about 26% (Aug 2025) to 76% (May 2026) to about 91% (Sep 2026), judged by Claude. Its LLM-training optimization speedup went from about 3x (Opus 4) to 17x, 34x and 52x (Mythos Preview), against about 4x for a skilled human in 4-8 h. Self-reported uplift went from 1.2x to 12x. OpenAI reports 3.1 agent-workdays per human workday by mid-Aug 2026. Formal thresholds have still not been crossed by any lab's own determination. OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra is below High for AI self-improvement (Research Debugging 78.05%). Google lists ML R&D acceleration and automation CCLs as not reached for Gemini 4 Argon, with 90% on its internal RE-Bench as the decision line. Anthropic says no model exceeds its threshold, though its S-1/A says it "may imminently meet" it. On weight self-editing: SEAL (MIT, Jun 2025) did have small models update their own weights by writing their own fine-tuning data, but in a narrow research setting. The Nov 2026 "weight-space programming" post had GPT-6 Astra edit a different, tiny model (Qwen3.5-0.8B). Darwin Gödel Machine (2025) and Mendel Gödel Machine (Aug 2026) rewrite agent code, not weights. Data caveat: WebFetch's own summary of METR's YAML wrongly multiplied the values by 60. I checked the raw file: the values are in minutes, and the minute figures in this report are corrected.

findings.claim: METR's independent assessment, using Anthropic's internal data, finds Anthropic's rate of capability improvement on well-specified tasks roughly doubled after Oct 2025.
findings.value: AECI slope about +15 pts/yr before vs about +29 pts/yr after a 2025-10-07 breakpoint; acceleration 1.9x [95% CI 1.5-2.8x]; robustness range 1.1x (cloglog) to 2.9x (log-log); 1.4x (+17 to +24 pts/yr) including all frontier developers; about 80% of acceleration guessed due to AI; internal Model 4 AECI 178.6 (179.7 after dropping 3 benchmarks); Model 4 above 50% on all 15 AECI benchmarks
findings.source_title: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026 (METR)
findings.notes: Independent analysis, but Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence METR found most informative, and METR had no sampling access to unreleased models. METR's acceleration estimate (1.9x) is computed on AECI, Anthropic's internal version of the ECI, which is not on the same scale as Epoch's public ECI. Engagement ran Aug 12 - Oct 29, 2026. Anthropic's own Haiku 5.5 card estimated 1.7x. This directly answers the user's question: the claim that public data shows no re-acceleration must be updated.

No frontier lab reports a model editing its own weights directly. Weight-space blog: https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/ (unreviewed; authors say editing 'could not add an ability the model lacked').

frontier_aa.summary:
Main conclusion: the Artificial Analysis (AA) Intelligence Index can't be the one consistent metric for the three snapshots (2025-11-07, 2026-05-07, 2026-11-07). The index went through v3.0 (Sep 2025), v4.0 (Jan 2026), v4.1 to v4.3.2 (Jun to Oct 2026), v5.0 (27 Oct 2026) and v5.0.1 (Nov 2026). AA's methodology page says scores are only comparable within a version. Today the live AA pages show only v5.0.1, which covers roughly Mar 2026 onward. GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5.2 and DeepSeek V3.2 all show 'N/A'. I could not fetch archived AA leaderboards because web.archive.org is blocked for the fetch tool.

The best consistent capability scale I found is Epoch AI's Capabilities Index (ECI). Epoch's CSV (updated 2026-11-07) scores every model from GPT-4.1/o3-era 2025 releases through GPT-6.1 Terra (2026-10-26) on one statistically stitched scale, with 95% confidence intervals. I paired ECI with list input/output prices taken from each model's AA page. I computed my own blended price at a 3:1 input:output ratio. AA's displayed 'blended' figure now uses a 7:2:1 cache-hit:input:output ratio, so I did not use it.

Result: 55 models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Zhipu/Z.ai and Alibaba. Meta and Mistral models have ECI scores, but I fetched no prices for them.

Rough frontier read-out from this data (my own calculation; check before publishing):
- **Equal capability:** in Nov 2025, GPT-5 scored ECI 150.0 at $3.44 blended. By May 2026, Gemini 3 Flash scored 152.25 at $1.125. By Nov 2026, DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 scored 154.34 at $0.175 (open weights). That is about 20x cheaper per token in 12 months.
- **Equal price (at or under about $3.50 blended):** the best score rose from 150.0 (GPT-5, Nov 2025) to 152.25 (Gemini 3 Flash, May 2026) to 167.82 (GPT-6.1 Terra at $2.00, Nov 2026).
- **Cheapest tier:** Claude Haiku 5.5 ($0.10/$0.50 per million tokens, ECI 160.22) now beats GPT-5.5 from April 2026 (ECI 160.04 at $11.25 blended).
- **Top of the market:** the top price point is still high. GPT-6 Astra is $10/$50 per million tokens (ECI 169.07), and Claude Fable 5 is $10/$50.

Big caveat: per-token prices leave out how many tokens each model uses. AA's per-task cost figures show cost varying 10x or more between reasoning settings of the same model (Claude Opus 5.5: $0.98 at low effort, $10.04 at max). So per-token Pareto charts should be labelled 'list price', or cross-checked with AA cost-per-task inside v5 only.

Existing analyses to cite:
- **Epoch, 'The plunging price of thought' (Emberson & Roodman, 2026-09-22):** cost to reach a fixed score falls 47% per quarter, about 13x per year. The method counts reasoning tokens. Its interactive site has 'isocost' (best accuracy at a fixed budget over time) and 'pareto_frontier' (one staircase per half-year) figures, which is essentially the chart the author wants.
- **Gundlach et al., arXiv 2511.23455:** price at a fixed benchmark score falls 5 to 10x per year at the frontier, while the price of running frontier models rises 3 to 18x per year.
- **AA articles:** the v4.3 announcement, the v5 announcement, 'GPT-6 Sol and Luna push the cost efficiency frontier' and the 2026-07-17 frontier article.

LMArena (now arena.ai) gives a second single-scale option. Its text Elo is recomputed for all 419 models (snapshot 2026-11-06). But it measures user preference, not capability, and its listed prices often disagree with AA (often exactly half).

frontier_aa.metric_choice:
I recommend the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI, epoch.ai/data/eci_scores.csv, updated 2026-11-07) as the single capability metric, not the AA Intelligence Index.

Why not the AA index: it changed version at least five times inside the window (v3.0 Sep 2025, v4.0 Jan 2026, v4.1 Jun 2026, v4.2/4.3 Sep 2026, v5.0 27 Oct 2026, v5.0.1 Nov 2026). The current v5.0.1 does not score 2025 models; GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2 all show N/A. Stable AA sub-benchmarks also fail. GPQA Diamond was dropped from the index in v4.2 and is saturated (about 96%). HLE was dropped in v5.0.

Why ECI: it puts every model from early 2025 to late Oct 2026 on one recomputed scale (GPT-5 = 150 anchor), with 95% confidence intervals, so 'equal capability' and 'better' are defined consistently across all three snapshots. LMArena/arena.ai text Elo is the only other single-scale option, but it measures preference.

Cost: I used each model's list price per million input and output tokens from its Artificial Analysis model page, for the first-party API or the median across providers for open models. I blended these myself at 3:1 input:output: (3 × input + output) / 4. I did not use AA's displayed 'blended' price, which now uses a 7:2:1 cache-hit:input:output ratio.

AA cost to run the index (which includes reasoning tokens) would be preferable, but it exists only within an index version. Under v5 it covers only about Mar 2026 onward, so it can serve as a robustness check for the Nov 2026 snapshot only.

Label the chart 'list price per token', and add the caveat that real cost per task also depends on tokens used (10x or more variation by effort level).

checks.claim: MIT CSAIL 'Sparks of Weight-Space Programming' (2 Nov 2026): GPT-6 Astra edited Qwen3.5-0.8B weights with no gradient descent, using a Python kernel and up to 50 forward passes; it edited 131,072 weights (0.016%). MATH-500 7.9%->48.1%, GSM8K 13.8%->67.1%, IFEval 21.0%->62.3%, token-limit hits 93%->33.1% (limit 32,768).
checks.correct_value: All numbers match the primary post. Authors are Rikiya Takehi*, Jayden Teoh*, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab (MIT CSAIL), dated 2 Nov 2026. The Qwen kernel had no GPU and allowed 10, 25 or 50 forward passes. Token-limit hits stayed at 87.2% with 10 passes and 86.4% with 25 passes. The BibTeX calls it a 'Blog post'.
checks.note: Lab-reported, not peer-reviewed. The model being edited is a different, much smaller model, not Astra. The logs repo exists (github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs, CC BY 4.0) and says Astra ran through the Codex CLI at high, xhigh or max reasoning effort.

checks.claim: Gemma 3 270M: Astra's edits did not improve math (MATH-500 6.8% base vs ~7.0-7.7% edited); 'could not add an ability the model lacked'
checks.correct_value: Base 6.8%. Edited: 7.0% (5 passes), 7.6% (10), 7.7% (25), 7.0% (50). Gemma's base token-limit hit rate was 8.5%, with an 8,192-token limit, so it had no looping problem to remove.
checks.note: The quote is verbatim. Note that Gemma had a different token limit (8,192 vs Qwen's 32,768).

checks.claim: From-scratch writing (no tools): MinAtar Breakout 517.4 vs PPO 15.8 (100M)/25.3 (500M); Seaquest 53.1 vs 5.6/88.9; Asterix 53.2 vs 25.8/55.2; Kinetix 0%->100% over 1,024 episodes, changing 3.5% of 171,664 weights
checks.correct_value: The MinAtar numbers are exact. Kinetix: the PPO network succeeded in 0 of 256 episodes, and Astra's edit succeeded in 1,024 of 1,024. The 0% and 100% come from different episode counts.
checks.note: Kinetix is a one-shot edit of an existing PPO network (Exp 4), not writing from scratch, so it should not sit under a 'from scratch' heading. Astra beats PPO-500M only on Breakout (about 20.4x). Breakout 'no tools, one reply' is correct for Exp 5.

checks.claim: The authors do not claim recursive self-improvement; results 'very early', capabilities 'still limited'
checks.correct_value: The post calls them 'very early results' and capabilities 'still limited, specifically due to inefficiencies in context length and harnesses'. It treats models editing their own weights as a future possibility.
checks.note: When quoting 'still limited', keep the rest of the clause: the authors blame harness and context length, not a lack of capability.

checks.claim: Hugging Face rerun (akhaliq, ML Intern on HF Jobs): MATH-500 51.0% (500x4, H200), 31.6% token-limit; base smoke test 5.0% (25 problems); edit = 64 down_proj columns in MLP layers 15 and 19, only two tensors differ
checks.correct_value: 51.0% and 31.6% on 500 problems x 4 samples (2,000 generations, about 43.4M tokens, 51 min, H200, vLLM). The base smoke test scored 5.0% on 25 problems, with 95% hitting the limit. Only the tensors layers.15/19.mlp.down_proj.weight differ. Dated 2 Nov 2026.
checks.note: Two caveats on calling it 'independent'. First, the card says akhaliq built the checkpoint itself (a multimodal export 'duplicated from' ML-Intern-lab) as well as the rerun. Second, it used its own sampling settings (presence_penalty 1.5, temp 0.6). So it independently re-evaluates the released weights but does not re-derive the edit. The 5.0% base figure comes from only 25 problems and is noisy, so it should not be compared directly with 7.9%.

selfweights_landscape.overall:
The main claims hold up against primary sources. The MIT post's numbers are exact: 131,072 weights (0.016%); MATH-500 7.9 to 48.1; GSM8K, IFEval and token-limit figures; Gemma 6.8 to 7.0-7.7; the MinAtar scores. So are the HF rerun (51.0%), Willison, Goedecke, SEAL, MASS, O'Neill, FutureSearch, Cursor, DGM, AlphaEvolve and the venue claims. The summary's caution about NeurIPS and WeightLoop was right.

Corrections needed:
1. Honnibal counts 2 write-from-zero rows (Exps 5 and 6), not 1. Exp 5 was also tool-free, so 4 of 10 rows used no tools, not 3.
2. Kinetix PPO failed in 0 of 256 episodes, while Astra's edit succeeded in 1,024 of 1,024. The baselines use different episode counts, and Kinetix is an edit (Exp 4), not writing from scratch.
3. Goedecke's phrase is 'smart human ML researcher', not 'competent'.
4. The HF 'independent' rerun re-evaluates the released checkpoint with different sampling settings. akhaliq also built that checkpoint export, and the rerun does not re-derive the edit. The 5.0% base figure comes from only 25 problems and should not be set against 7.9%.

Secondary-only items, not verified against originals:
- Krentsel's cross-generation multipliers (OfficeChai describing an X chart, no sample sizes). Astra's 22x differs from MIT's own 20.4x.
- The Zhihu figures (576/579, 1,152 held-out, 10.6 to 60.4) come via Latent Space only. The logs README has no 1,152-problem held-out set.
Label both as secondary and unreplicated, and do not chart them as precise.

Context to add:
- MASS gains are per output token, with no gains on SWE-bench Verified or Terminal-Bench.
- SEAL loses to GPT-4.1 synthetic data in its continued-pretraining settings.

The bottom-line framing ('not editing their own weights; with tools, patch small other models like a skilled researcher') is supported.

I fetched the METR assessment, METR's risk-report review, METR's TH1.1 post, METR's time-horizons page, three Epoch pages, Jonas Moss's post and SEC EDGAR full-text search. No numbers look fabricated. Corrections needed:
(1) S-1 language: "may not identify a significant acceleration… until after it has occurred" is still in the S-1/A, per EDGAR full-text search. The amendment added the "may imminently meet" language; it did not replace the old sentence. Also, the S-1/A text found by full-text search reads "have not designated", not "haven't".

I checked 20 claims. The core load-bearing claims hold against primary sources: the METR Nov 5, 2026 Anthropic assessment (every number), the METR TH1.1 raw YAML values (minutes, consistent with the ~12 h public frontier), the Epoch ECI CSV frontier through GPT-6 Astra 169.07, Epoch's slope estimates, the Google AI-code quotes, and the Anthropic Institute figures. The self-reported uplift series joins Slack polls to a survey. Release dates differ across METR and Epoch (o1: Dec 5 vs Dec 17, 2024). AECI is not on the public ECI scale, and ECI snapshots from before and after the Nov 4 methodology change are not comparable.
(4) MLE-bench is developer-submitted on an OpenAI benchmark, not truly independent.

(6) The 17x/34x speedups are from a third-party wiki only. The 52x Mythos figure carries a reported reward-hacking caveat.

frontier_aa.overall: The core dataset is solid. All 25 ECI scores, credible intervals and dates match Epoch's eci_scores.csv exactly (files dated Nov 7, 2026). The 14 spot-checked prices match AA's pages or articles, and 12 release dates agree between Epoch and AA. The AA version history, leaderboard, v5 announcement and July 2026 article numbers are accurate. The Epoch 13x/yr figure (47%/quarter 'since 2023', 22 Sep 2026) and the Gundlach et al. 5–10x/yr and 3–18x/yr figures are confirmed. The 7:2:1 blend definition is confirmed and checks out arithmetically. Problems to fix before publishing: (1) AA's methodology page does NOT state that index scores are comparable only within a version; this is our own inference. The v5 article likewise does not say per-task costs are incomparable across versions. (2) Epoch's 725x example says o3 was released 31 Jan 2025, but o3 came out 16 Apr 2025 (per Epoch's own CSV and AA), so the 'under 18 months' span and the baseline model conflict. Don't quote it as-is. (3) May 2026 equal-price frontier: Grok 4.20 (152.27, $1.56 blended) ties Gemini 3 Flash, so report about 152 as a tie. (4) 'Haiku 5.5 beats GPT-5.5' is inside the intervals; say 'matches'. (5) Use Fable 5.1, not the deprecated Fable 5, for Nov 2026. (6) The ~20x equal-capability figure rests on DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731's median third-party price on a deprecated model; give GPT-6 Luna or Haiku 5.5 at $0.20 (about 17x) as a closed-model cross-check, and label the mixed price bases. (7) 'Google doubling Gemini prices on 1 Dec' applies only to Gemini 4 Argon; Flash models follow on 1 Jan 2027. (8) Epoch calls its ranges 'credible intervals' with no stated level, so do not call them 95% CIs. (9) Gemini 4 Carbon (the AA #1) is not in ECI or Google's pricing page and is preliminary on Arena; treat it as provisional. None of the figures look invented. The misdating, if any, is in the Epoch article itself.
